takeaways: Jason and team agent Zach Bidleman break cash offers into three types. As-is (leave whatever you want behind) usually pays the least; empty and broom-clean pays a bit more; and a two-closing program usually pays the most.

In a two-closing program, the investor pays part of the agreed amount up front (about 65% in Zach's example), renovates and resells, then pays the rest at resale, often with a share of any gain above the target price. If it sells for less, you get less, and the first payment may not cover your mortgage.
Every lien on the title gets paid at closing: mortgages, mechanic's liens, utility or medical liens, child support and so on. Tell your agent about them early so you know your real net.

The upside of a cash offer is speed (closing in as little as about 7 days), no repairs and few or no showings. The downside: investors are businesses, and offers can come in up to 25% to 30% below open-market value.

Insist on a standard Minnesota purchase agreement and proof of funds, and have a lawyer review anything unusual. Watch for clauses like "subject to board approval" or a buyer's right to cancel at any time.

Cash offers often fit inherited homes owned by out-of-state heirs, or homes needing major repairs. If you'd grade your home a 6 or better out of 10 and aren't in a hurry, the open market usually nets more.

faq.q: Should I take a cash offer on my house?
faq.a: It can make sense if the home needs major work, you inherited it from out of state, or speed and convenience matter most. If the home is in good shape and you have time, listing on the open market usually nets more. Compare both side by side.

faq.q: How much less is a cash offer than market value?
faq.a: It varies by investor, but the video says offers can come in up to 25% to 30% below what the home could sell for on the open market, because the investor pays for repairs and resale and needs a profit.

faq.q: What is a two-closing cash offer?
faq.a: The investor pays part of the price at a first closing, renovates and resells the home, then pays you the rest at resale. It usually pays the most of the cash options but depends on the resale price.

takeaways: As of mid-November 2025, the Twin Cities had more than 10,000 active listings, about 2.7 months of supply: more choice for buyers than at any time since the pandemic, though still short of a traditional balanced market.
By type: single-family homes had about 2.5 months of supply, townhomes about 3 and condos about 5, making condos the softest segment. Downtown Saint Paul condos averaged about 99 days on market.

Builders are the big competition: about two-thirds offer strong incentives, such as rate buydowns near 5% versus 6.25% to 6.5% for resale, worth $20,000 to $40,000 or more. Dated homes that need work are hit hardest.

Buyers: concessions, repair credits, home warranties and inspections are back. Target homes on the market 25 to 40 days, compare monthly payments rather than list prices, and budget $10,000 to $25,000 for new-construction extras like decks, landscaping and blinds.
A seller-paid rate buydown of about $15,000 can lower your payment more than a $30,000 price cut, according to Jason.

Sellers: the first two weeks decide most of the outcome. Homes priced about 5% over market sat about 60 days longer on average. Paint, lighting and carpet pay off, and a price $20,000 to $40,000 below comparable new construction, or a buydown offer, helps you compete.
Move-in-ready homes in popular suburbs still sold in about 14 to 23 days when priced right, and luxury homes over $1 million saw days on market drop about 10%.

faq.q: Is the Twin Cities housing market slowing down?
faq.a: It's more balanced, not crashing. Inventory rose to about 2.7 months of supply in late 2025, bidding wars are rarer, and condos are softest, but well-priced, move-in-ready homes in popular suburbs still sell in two to three weeks.

faq.q: Is a rate buydown better than a price cut?
faq.a: Often, for your monthly payment. Jason notes a $15,000 seller-paid buydown can lower the payment more than a $30,000 price reduction. Run both with your lender.

takeaways: Today's luxury buyers spending about $800,000 to $2 million are choosing space, privacy and lifestyle over historic addresses, according to Jason. Seven communities, with prices as stated in the video:
Wayzata (median around $1.3 million): a walkable village on Lake Minnetonka with public docks, marinas and lakeside dining. Social and visible rather than private.
Chanhassen (median around $600,000, new construction into the low $800,000s): newer homes, cul-de-sacs, trails and parks like Lake Ann and Lake Susan.
Credit River (median in the low $900,000s): became a city in 2021 to stay rural, with wooded acreage, room for outbuildings and horses, and shopping in Prior Lake, Savage and Lakeville.
Summit Avenue in Saint Paul (upper $700,000s to over $1.5 million): historic homes, mature trees and the Mississippi River Boulevard trails near downtown.
Prior Lake (everyday homes in the low $400,000s to high $500,000s, lakefront and custom $1 million and up): public beaches, fishing piers and Lakefront Park.

Maple Grove (typical home in the high $400,000s, higher-end from the high $500,000s to low $700,000s): Arbor Lakes, a growing community center and everything within about 10 minutes. Excelsior (around the mid-$800,000s): a one-square-mile walkable village on Lake Minnetonka with The Commons park and lake cruises.

faq.q: What are the best luxury suburbs in the Twin Cities?
faq.a: Jason highlights Wayzata, Chanhassen, Credit River, Summit Avenue in Saint Paul, Prior Lake, Maple Grove and Excelsior, each offering a different trade-off between lake access, privacy, space and convenience.

faq.q: Where can I buy acreage near the Twin Cities?
faq.a: Credit River in Scott County is one option: a rural city with wooded acreage lots and custom homes, with a median in the low $900,000s at the time of the video, close to Prior Lake, Savage and Lakeville.

takeaways: Twin Cities builders are cutting prices, mostly on finished, unsold "spec" or inventory homes, because every month an empty home sits costs them interest, taxes, insurance and upkeep. Homes you order and wait for rarely get the same cuts.

Nationally, about four in 10 builders cut prices late last year, by about 5% on average, and about two-thirds offered incentives. Lennar's annual filing showed an average incentive of about $62,700 per home, up from $48,800.

Three kinds of savings: a straight price cut (a smaller loan), a rate buydown (a lower payment, same loan) and a flexible credit toward closing costs or upgrades. Offers may require the builder's lender and may not stack.

Examples at the time of the video: a Lennar home at Watermark in Lino Lakes about $52,000 off (just under $500,000, roughly $350 a month less), a Lennar home at Crow River Heights in Hanover about $39,000 off, and a Pulte home at Amber Fields in Rosemount about $38,000 off.

By comparison, Twin Cities resale homes sold for about 98% of asking in August, roughly $8,000 off a $400,000 home. Builder deals are tied to specific homes and change quickly, so confirm what's current.

faq.q: Are Twin Cities builders cutting prices?
faq.a: Yes, mostly on finished homes that haven't sold. In the video, cuts of about $38,000 to $52,000 were found in Lino Lakes, Hanover and Rosemount, while to-be-built floor plans had no discount.

faq.q: What's the difference between a builder price cut and a rate buydown?
faq.a: A price cut lowers the amount you borrow for good. A rate buydown lowers your rate and payment, but the loan amount stays the same. A credit usually goes toward closing costs or upgrades.

takeaways: A 2022 overview of Eden Prairie, on the southwest side of the metro: about 64,000 residents, an average commute of about 24 minutes and a median house price around $450,000 at the time. See the market report for current prices.
Restaurants cluster around Eden Prairie Center and beyond, from Redstone to Kona Grill. Southdale in neighboring Edina was the first fully enclosed mall in the country.
Eden Prairie has 15 lakes; Bryant and Mitchell are full recreational lakes for boating and water sports.
There are 37 city parks, plus Bryant Lake Regional Park and Purgatory Park. Red Rock Lake Park has boating in summer and hockey rinks on the ice in winter.
Getting around: Highway 212, I-494 and Highway 169, plus bus service, with the Green Line light rail extension under construction to end in Eden Prairie.

faq.q: How many lakes are in Eden Prairie?
faq.a: 15, according to the video. Bryant Lake and Mitchell Lake are full recreational lakes for boating and water sports.

faq.q: Will the light rail go to Eden Prairie?
faq.a: Yes. The Green Line Extension (Southwest light rail) ends in Eden Prairie.

takeaways: A lighthearted 2022 list of "10 reasons not to live in Minnesota," most with an upside. Winter is cold, but summers (roughly mid-May to mid-September) are beautiful and fall color is spectacular.
Mosquitoes come with the lakes, but Metropolitan Mosquito Control keeps them in check.
Wildlife is everywhere, and seasonal allergies can be a challenge with all the trees and flowers.
Traffic is light for a metro this size, but the area is spread out: it can take about an hour and a half to cross from one side of the Twin Cities to the other.

Road construction follows every winter, "Minnesota nice" is real, and hail is common enough that many roofs get replaced through insurance. Tornadoes are more common farther south, toward the Iowa border.
State income tax rates are relatively high (today 5.35% to 9.85%), which Jason ties to clean, well-run cities and quick snow removal.

faq.q: What are the downsides of living in Minnesota?
faq.a: Cold winters, mosquitoes, seasonal allergies, constant summer road construction, hail and relatively high state income taxes. Most come with an upside, such as four real seasons and well-maintained cities.
Not compared with most large metros, according to Jason. The bigger issue is distance: the metro is spread out, and summer road construction can slow commutes.
